name: Squintmaxxing
lead: Squintmaxxing is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person habitually narrows the eyelids slightly, aiming for the look community members call "hunter eyes": a lower upper eyelid line and a more intense, less wide-open gaze. Proponents describe it as a free, instant adjustment that can make the eye area look more attractive [1][2].

Squinting itself is a documented behaviour. Wikipedia notes it can briefly sharpen vision in people with uncorrected refractive error, and an ophthalmologist quoted there says the belief that squinting damages eyesight is an old wives' tale, with temporary headache from muscle tension the only harm cited [3]. No studies have tested whether deliberate squinting changes perceived attractiveness.

paras: A widely shared looksmax.org guide describes the technique as opening the eyes wide and then relaxing them to a slight squint, similar to the reflex in bright sun, and says it should be mild and held often until it becomes unconscious [1]. The same guide warns against an exaggerated squint that wrinkles the face [1]. A separate thread jokingly lists "professional permasquinters" and says the look suits certain eye shapes and medial canthus types, with the caution to proceed carefully [2].

One looksmax.org thread asks whether squinting could contribute to hair loss at the temples, with users reporting anecdotes about temple balding and tense muscles around the eye [4]. No published research supports a link between squinting and balding.

Squinting reduces light entering the eye and filters off-axis rays, which can briefly sharpen vision for people with uncorrected refractive error; it is also a reflex in bright light, especially for light-coloured eyes [3]. Wikipedia reports that ophthalmologist Robert MacLaren describes the idea that squinting worsens eyesight as an old wives' tale [3]. Persistent squinting beyond a short adjustment period in a healthy eye can indicate photophobia [3].

lore.intro: Squintmaxxing is promoted on looksmax.org as a free, instant improvement; discussion is mostly threads of guides and jokes rather than data [1][2].

claims.claim: A slight squint gives "hunter eyes" and a boost to appearance ratings
claims.believers: Posters say a relaxed partial squint lowers the upper lid and creates a more intense look, calling it an easy looksmax [1][2].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether habitual squinting changes how attractive a face is rated.

claims.claim: Squinting too much could harm the face or hair
claims.believers: Some users report worrying about temple hair loss or wrinkles from sustained squinting [1][4].
claims.experts: No published studies link squinting to hair loss; an ophthalmologist quoted by Wikipedia cites only temporary headache as a harm of squinting [3].

card.summary: Habitually narrowing the eyes for a "hunter" look; free, reversible and untested.
card.note: No studies on appearance effects; community claims about hair loss are unsupported by research.

quick.overview:
Squintmaxxing means slightly narrowing the eyelids, often, to get a more intense "hunter eyes" look. It costs nothing and can be stopped at any time.

It is promoted on looksmax.org, but no research has tested whether it changes perceived attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Narrowing the lids lowers the visible upper eyelid line and reduces the amount of eye shown. Proponents say this changes the impression of the eye area.
quick.risks: Squinting is generally regarded as harmless, with temporary headache from muscle tension the harm cited by an ophthalmologist. Forum claims about wrinkles or temple balding have no published support.
